entries.meaning: The default coordinator: it adds, and it will add anything to anything as long as the two halves are the same grammatical kind. Beyond plain addition it carries sequence (She got up and left), result (He tripped and fell), and, after an imperative, a condition (Move and I'll shoot means "if you move"). Of all the addition words it is the only one that makes a subject genuinely plural — plus is informal and as well as leaves the verb alone.
examples: She ordered a salad and a glass of iced tea.
We packed the car, and the kids were asleep before we hit the highway.
Add the flour, the sugar, and a pinch of salt.
Say that one more time and I'm leaving.
He came home, dropped his bag, and went straight to bed.
And then, out of nowhere, the power went out.
entries.русский: и — основной соединительный союз: добавление, последовательность, результат
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: coordinating
entries.clause type: coordinate clause; also joins words and phrases of any rank
entries.pattern: [X] and [Y]. · [X], [Y], and [Z]. · [independent clause], and [independent clause]. · [imperative] and [result]. · And [clause]. (sentence-initial)
entries.punctuation: No comma between two joined words, phrases, or verbs sharing one subject (bread and butter; She stood up and left). Comma before and when it joins two independent clauses (She called, and I answered), droppable when both clauses are very short. In a list of three or more, American editing puts a serial comma before the final and (red, white, and blue).
entries.variants: & (ampersand — company names, notes, informal writing) · 'n' (rock 'n' roll, mac 'n' cheese) · reduced /ən/ in ordinary speech
entries.see also: and/or, and so, and then, and yet, plus, as well as, or, both … and

entries.meaning: Marks the second element as running against what the first led you to expect. It is the plain, neutral contrast word, and the differences around it are worth memorizing: yet adds a note of "in spite of that," however means the same but is an adverb and needs a semicolon before it, and although subordinates instead of coordinating, which changes which half of the sentence carries the point.
examples: I called twice, but nobody picked up.
The soup was bland but filling.
It's not the money but the principle.
But nobody had checked the budget.
She said she'd think about it, but I could tell she had already decided.
We can go Friday but not Saturday.
entries.русский: но, а — второе идёт вразрез с тем, чего ждёшь после первого
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: coordinating (also a preposition meaning "except", and an adverb in fixed phrases)
entries.clause type: coordinate clause; also joins words and phrases
entries.pattern: [X] but [Y]. · [independent clause], but [independent clause]. · not [X] but [Y]. · But [clause]. (sentence-initial)
entries.punctuation: Comma before but when it joins two independent clauses (I called, but nobody answered). No comma when it joins two words or phrases (small but tidy). In the not X but Y frame the comma is optional and marks emphasis (It's not the money, but the principle). No comma after But at the head of a sentence unless what follows is itself parenthetical.
entries.variants: but then · but rather · but also (in not only … but also) · prepositional but (everyone but me) is a different word class
entries.see also: yet, and yet, but then, but rather, only, however, although

entries.meaning: Supplies a reason or a justification for what was just said — roughly because or since, but grammatically a coordinator. In American English it is close to literary now: outside scripture, older fiction, and deliberately elevated prose, people say because. Its behavior is unlike because too — its clause cannot be moved ahead of the main clause (For she had never lied to me, I trusted her is impossible), it cannot answer why?, and it cannot be the focus of a cleft.
examples: I trusted her, for she had never lied to me.
We turned back, for the trail had washed out below the ridge.
Do not weep, for the child is not dead but sleeping.
He spoke slowly, for he wanted every word to land.
The town emptied out in October, for there was no work to be had after the harvest.
She kept the letters, for they were all she had left of him.
He refused the money. For he had given his word, and that was the end of it.
entries.русский: ибо, ведь — книжн./устар. союз причины; всегда с запятой перед ним
entries.register: formal, literary
entries.type: coordinating (far more often a preposition — a gift for you — and the marker of infinitival clauses: for her to leave now would be rude)
entries.clause type: coordinate clause of reason
entries.pattern: [independent clause], for [independent clause]. — normally medial · For [clause]. (sentence-initial; scripture and consciously elevated prose only, linking back to the sentence before)
entries.punctuation: Always put a comma before conjunctive for; without one the word reads as the preposition (He waited for the bus vs. He waited, for the bus was late). It never joins anything smaller than a clause. Sentence-initial For belongs to scripture and deliberately elevated writing (For the wages of sin is death), where it points back across the period and takes no comma after it.
entries.variants: none as a conjunction · prepositional for (a gift for you) is a different word class · infinitival for (for her to leave now would be rude)
entries.see also: so, and so, because, since, therefore

entries.meaning: Adds a second negative to a negative already on the table: "and not that either." Two traps come with it. Word order inverts (nor did he call, never nor he called), and the clause takes no second not, because nor already carries the negation.
examples: He didn't call, nor did he answer my texts.
The company never admitted fault, nor did it offer a refund.
Neither the manager nor the assistants were told about the merger.
She isn't unkind, nor is she especially warm.
I have no time for this, nor the patience.
Nor should we forget who paid for the road in the first place.
entries.русский: и не, также не — второе отрицание; требует инверсии: nor did he call
entries.register: formal to neutral
entries.type: coordinating (also the second half of the correlative neither … nor)
entries.clause type: coordinate clause, negative
entries.pattern: [negative clause], nor [auxiliary or be] [subject] [rest]. · neither [X] nor [Y]. · [negative clause], nor [noun phrase]. (with the verb gapped) · Nor [auxiliary] [subject] … (sentence-initial, formal)
entries.punctuation: Comma before nor when it joins two independent clauses (He didn't call, nor did he write). No comma inside a neither … nor pair joining words or phrases (neither hot nor cold). The clause after clause-linking nor is inverted — auxiliary or be before the subject. Sentence-initial Nor follows a period or a semicolon, inverts the same way, and takes no comma after it.
entries.variants: neither … nor (correlative) · nor yet (literary, archaic)
entries.see also: or, and, much less, neither … nor, either … or

entries.meaning: Offers an alternative. English or is normally inclusive — coffee or tea does not forbid both — and only context or an explicit either … or forces the exclusive reading. Two side jobs are worth learning: after an imperative it states the consequence of not complying, and after a comma it renames the thing just mentioned. Note also that after a negative it is or, not and, that spreads the negation: I don't eat meat or fish.
examples: Do you want the aisle or the window?
We could drive, or we could fly.
Would you rather have coffee, tea, or something cold?
Hurry up, or we'll miss the last train.
I don't eat meat or fish.
She studies the humerus, or upper arm bone, in the first week of the course.
Either you tell him or I will.
entries.русский: или — альтернатива, обычно невзаимоисключающая (можно и то и другое)
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: coordinating
entries.clause type: coordinate clause; also joins words and phrases
entries.pattern: [X] or [Y]. · [X], [Y], or [Z]. · [independent clause], or [independent clause]. · [imperative], or [consequence]. · either [X] or [Y]. · [term], or [other name for the same thing], …
entries.punctuation: No comma between two joined words or phrases (coffee or tea). Comma before or joining two independent clauses (Hurry, or we'll miss it), droppable only when both clauses are very short. Serial comma before the final or in a list of three or more (by car, by train, or by bus). A comma before or also signals the renaming use, and a second comma closes it (the humerus, or upper arm bone, is …).
entries.variants: or else · or rather · and/or · either … or (correlative)
entries.see also: and/or, or else, or rather, nor, and, versus, either … or, whether

entries.meaning: States the result of what came before: cause first, effect after so. It is the mirror image of because, which puts the effect first and the cause second. The high-value distinction is against so (that): I left early, so I beat traffic reports what happened, while I left early so I could beat traffic reports what was intended.
examples: Traffic was terrible, so we missed the opening.
The store was out of basil, so I used parsley.
He never wrote back, so I stopped emailing.
I left early so I could beat the traffic.
So, what did the doctor say?
She's allergic to cats, so we met at my place instead.
entries.русский: поэтому, так что — следствие: сначала причина, потом результат
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: coordinating (also subordinating in so that, a degree adverb, and a discourse marker)
entries.clause type: coordinate clause of result
entries.pattern: [independent clause], so [independent clause]. · So [clause]. (conversational opener) · compare subordinating [clause] so (that) [purpose clause]. — no comma
entries.punctuation: Comma before so when it joins two independent clauses (It rained, so we stayed in). No comma when so means "so that" and introduces a purpose (I left early so I could beat traffic) — the presence or absence of that comma is the main clue to which reading is intended. Sentence-initial discourse So takes a comma after it only as a conversational aside (So, what happened?).
entries.variants: and so · so that (subordinating, purpose) · so … that (correlative, degree)
entries.see also: and so, for, therefore, so that, because

entries.meaning: Contrast plus surprise: it asserts that both facts hold even though they look incompatible. But merely opposes; yet adds "and in spite of that." It is also one of only two FANBOYS words that ordinary usage lets you put and in front of — and yet and and so — a clue that both are half adverb; and but, and or, and and for are impossible in any variety, and and nor is British — American editing writes nor alone.
examples: She apologized, yet nothing actually changed.
The apartment is small yet surprisingly bright.
He had every reason to quit, yet he showed up every morning.
It was a simple question, yet nobody in the room could answer it.
Yet something about the story didn't add up.
She had barely known him and yet she cried through the whole service.
entries.русский: но всё же, и тем не менее — противопоставление с оттенком неожиданности
entries.register: neutral; a shade more formal than but in writing
entries.type: coordinating (also a time adverb: not yet, has she left yet?)
entries.clause type: coordinate clause of concessive contrast
entries.pattern: [X] yet [Y]. · [independent clause], yet [independent clause]. · [clause] and yet [clause]. · Yet [clause]. (sentence-initial)
entries.punctuation: Comma before yet when it joins two independent clauses (She apologized, yet nothing changed). No comma when it joins two words or phrases (firm yet fair). And yet takes the same comma. Sentence-initial Yet takes no comma after it.
entries.variants: and yet · adverbial yet (I haven't finished yet) is a different word class
entries.see also: but, and yet, but then, nevertheless, although

entries.meaning: A written shorthand for "either one or both," invented to close the loophole that inclusive or supposedly leaves open in contracts. Plain-language guides and many courts dislike it, since ordinary or is already inclusive and the slash breaks down past two items; the standard fix is X or Y or both.
examples: Bring a passport and/or a driver's license.
Applicants must show two years of experience and/or a relevant certificate.
The fee may be paid by the tenant and/or the guarantor.
Damage caused by fire and/or flooding is excluded from coverage.
Please copy your manager and/or the project lead on the final draft.
Signatures may be collected in person and/or electronically.
entries.русский: и/или — юр., канц.: «одно, другое или оба сразу»
entries.register: formal; legal, technical, and administrative writing
entries.type: coordinating (compound)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase; joins words and phrases, rarely clauses
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] and/or [noun phrase]. · [subject] and/or [subject] [verb] … · [verb phrase] and/or [verb phrase]. · [adjective] and/or [adjective]. · recommended rewrite: [X] or [Y] or both.
entries.punctuation: Written with a slash and no spaces around it. Punctuate the surrounding sentence exactly as you would for or: no comma between the two joined elements, none after the slash. Avoid it in a list of three or more, where its scope becomes genuinely ambiguous. Note too that subject–verb agreement after an and/or subject is unsettled (the tenant and/or the guarantor is — or are — liable), which is one more reason editors rewrite it.
entries.variants: and or (nonstandard spacing) · or/and (rare) · recommended rewrite: X or Y or both
entries.see also: or, and, or else, either … or

entries.meaning: The same result link as bare so, but heavier and more deliberate — it sums up rather than merely reports, which is why it lands so often at the end of a story or an argument. Keep it apart from additive and so with inversion (She was exhausted, and so was I), where so means "likewise" and is an adverb.
examples: The flight was canceled, and so we spent the night in Denver.
No one else volunteered, and so the job fell to me.
And so the summer ended, the way summers do.
The evidence never surfaced, and so the case was dropped.
We had promised the kids a beach day, and so a beach day is what they got.
The road washed out in April, and so the town was cut off for a week.
entries.русский: и потому, и вот — итоговое следствие, весомее простого so
entries.register: neutral; narrative or slightly formal
entries.type: coordinating (compound)
entries.clause type: coordinate clause of result
entries.pattern: [independent clause], and so [independent clause]. · And so [clause]. (sentence-initial, narrative)
entries.punctuation: Comma before and so when it joins two independent clauses; never a comma between and and so, and none after so. Sentence-initial And so takes no comma after it.
entries.variants: and therefore (formal) · do not confuse with and so + inversion (and so did I = "I did too")
entries.see also: so, and, and then, for, therefore

entries.meaning: Fixes the order of events, which plain and only implies. It has a second, rhetorical life in complaint and storytelling, where each and then stacks one new development on the last.
examples: We had dinner and then walked down to the water.
She read the letter twice and then put it back in the drawer.
First the check bounced, and then the landlord called.
And then he tells me the whole thing was my idea.
Boil the pasta, drain it, and then toss it with the sauce.
The power flickered twice and then went out for good.
entries.русский: а потом, и затем — закрепляет порядок событий, который and лишь подразумевает
entries.register: neutral; conversational in narrative
entries.type: coordinating (compound)
entries.clause type: coordinate clause of sequence
entries.pattern: [X] and then [Y]. · [subject] [verb phrase] and then [verb phrase]. · [independent clause], and then [independent clause]. · [X], [Y], and then [Z]. · And then [clause]. (sentence-initial)
entries.punctuation: No comma when and then joins two verb phrases sharing one subject (We had dinner and then walked down to the water). Comma before and then when it joins two independent clauses (First the check bounced, and then the landlord called) — the ordinary and rule, though fast narrative drops it between short clauses. Never a comma between and and then, and none after then; sentence-initial And then takes no comma either.
entries.variants: and then some (idiom: "and more besides") · and afterward (formal)
entries.see also: and, and so, or else, after, then

entries.meaning: Intensifies the surprise already in yet: it concedes the first fact and then registers the second as genuinely hard to square with it. English tolerates a doubled coordinator here only because yet is halfway to an adverb — the same license that produces and so — which is why and but and and or are impossible.
examples: He had every advantage, and yet he threw it away.
The book is barely two hundred pages and yet took him nine years to write.
She's been asked a hundred times, and yet she still answers as if it were new.
And yet nobody thought to check the basement.
The town has no industry left, and yet the population keeps growing.
It's the most obvious explanation, and yet it's wrong.
entries.русский: и всё же, и тем не менее — усиленное yet: признаёт первое и дивится второму
entries.register: neutral; common in writing
entries.type: coordinating (compound)
entries.clause type: coordinate clause of concessive contrast
entries.pattern: [independent clause], and yet [independent clause]. · [X] and yet [Y]. · And yet [clause]. (sentence-initial)
entries.punctuation: Comma before and yet between two independent clauses. Sentence-initial And yet normally takes no comma after it, though writers add one for a beat of hesitation.
entries.variants: and still · but still (looser, more conversational) · yet alone
entries.see also: yet, but, but then, and, nevertheless

entries.meaning: Replaces a rejected item with the correct one, so it needs a negative in front of it to do its work. Where plain but contrasts two things that can both be true, but rather cancels the first outright and substitutes the second.
examples: The problem wasn't the code but rather the data it was fed.
She didn't refuse, but rather asked for more time.
It's not that he's rude, but rather that he's completely unaware of other people.
We're not raising prices, but rather trimming the menu.
The delay wasn't caused by weather but rather by a paperwork error.
He isn't lazy but rather exhausted.
entries.русский: а (не X, а Y) — отменяет отвергнутое и подставляет верное; нужно отрицание впереди
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.type: coordinating (compound)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase or clause, corrective
entries.pattern: not [X] but rather [Y]. · [negative clause], but rather [corrected element]. · It is not that [clause] but rather that [clause].
entries.punctuation: In the not X but rather Y frame a comma before but rather is optional and adds emphasis; never a comma after it. When the first element is a full clause, use the comma.
entries.variants: but instead · but rather that · bare but · rather alone (not carelessness, rather fatigue — formal)
entries.see also: but, rather than, or rather, instead

entries.meaning: Introduces a second thought that softens or half-cancels what was just said — "on the other hand, this is also true." It differs from the purely temporal but then of narrative ("and after that"); the concessive one can always be replaced by but then again.
examples: The hotel was overpriced, but then everything downtown is.
She's never on time, but then neither am I.
I'd like to move somewhere warm — but then, I said that last year too.
But then again, he did warn us.
The sequel wasn't very good, but then the first one wasn't either.
He offered to pay, but then he always does.
entries.русский: но с другой стороны, впрочем — вторая мысль, смягчающая сказанное; разг.
entries.register: neutral; conversational
entries.type: coordinating (compound)
entries.clause type: coordinate clause, concessive afterthought
entries.pattern: [independent clause], but then [independent clause]. · [independent clause], but then again, [independent clause]. · But then [clause]. (sentence-initial)
entries.punctuation: Comma before but then. When but then again interrupts, fence it with a comma on each side. No comma after sentence-initial But then; a dash before it is a common alternative to the comma.
entries.variants: but then again · then again (on its own) · but on the other hand
entries.see also: but, yet, and then, only, however

entries.meaning: A reinforced nor: it adds one more negative and marks it as the least expected item of the set, the one a reader would have thought least likely. Hymns, scripture translations, and nineteenth-century prose use it freely; present-day American writing has all but dropped it, and bare nor carries the same load.
examples: He had no money, no prospects, nor yet any wish to acquire either.
She was not beautiful, nor yet plain.
The committee has no budget for this, nor yet the authority to ask for one.
I never learned my father's trade, nor yet wanted to.
The treaty settled neither the border, nor the fishing rights, nor yet the question of who would pay.
There was no answer at the door, nor yet a light in any of the windows.
entries.русский: и уж тем более не — устар., книжн.: усиленное nor
entries.register: formal, literary; archaic in flavor
entries.type: coordinating (compound; the reinforced form of nor)
entries.clause type: coordinate clause or phrase, negative
entries.pattern: [negative clause], nor yet [noun phrase]. · [negative clause], nor yet [auxiliary or be] [subject] [rest]. · neither [X], nor [Y], nor yet [Z]. · not [X], nor yet [Y].
entries.punctuation: Comma before nor yet, never one between the two words or after them. When a full clause follows, it inverts exactly as it does after bare nor (nor yet did he write). In a three-part negative list it marks the last item and takes the same comma the other items take.
entries.variants: nor (the plain modern form) · nor even · neither … nor · and not … either (plain-English rewrite)
entries.see also: nor, and yet, still less, yea, neither … nor

entries.meaning: States what will happen if the first clause is not carried out: a more explicitly consequential or. It is also the one coordinator in English that can survive with nothing after it at all, as an open-ended threat.
examples: Leave a note, or else they'll worry.
We need to leave by six, or else we'll hit rush hour.
Write it down, or else you'll forget by morning.
Pay the ticket by Friday or else it doubles.
Have the car back by ten — or else.
Book it now, or else the fare goes up.
entries.русский: а то, иначе — последствие или угроза при невыполнении первого
entries.register: neutral to informal
entries.type: coordinating (compound)
entries.clause type: coordinate clause of alternative consequence
entries.pattern: [imperative], or else [consequence]. · [independent clause], or else [independent clause]. · [warning] … or else. (elliptical threat)
entries.punctuation: Comma before or else when it joins two clauses; the comma is often dropped when the first clause is a short imperative. The bare threat Or else. stands as its own sentence and takes a period, and a dash before it is common.
entries.variants: bare else (literary) · otherwise (conjunctive adverb — takes a semicolon or a new sentence)
entries.see also: or, else, and/or, otherwise, unless

entries.meaning: Withdraws the word just used and substitutes a better one in mid-sentence. Unlike but rather, it needs no negative in front of it — it is correcting a statement the speaker has only just made.
examples: He's a colleague — or rather, he was, until last month.
We inherited a house, or rather a pile of lumber with a roof on it.
She agreed to help, or rather she didn't say no.
It's a diner, or rather, it was a diner in 1974 and nothing has been touched since.
I read the report, or rather I read the first two pages of it.
The meeting is Tuesday, or rather Wednesday now.
entries.русский: вернее, точнее — поправка к слову, только что сказанному самим говорящим
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: coordinating (compound)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase or clause, self-correcting
entries.pattern: [X], or rather, [more accurate X]. · [clause], or rather [restated clause]. · [clause] — or rather, [restated clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma before or rather, and a comma after it as well when a full clause follows. Dashes are common in place of the first comma, since the correction is parenthetical.
entries.variants: or, more precisely · or better · that is (formal) · I mean (spoken)
entries.see also: or, but rather, rather than, namely

entries.meaning: Adds a second party to the sentence without letting it into the subject, which is the whole reason to reach for it instead of and: The coach and two players were fined puts three people on the hook grammatically, while The coach, along with two players, was fined keeps the coach alone in the subject. It behaves exactly like as well as and together with for agreement, and unlike as well as it has no comparative twin to be confused with.
examples: The pitcher, along with two of the coaches, was ejected in the fourth inning.
She brought the signed contract along with a check for the deposit.
Bring a photo ID along with proof of address.
The fire took the barn along with everything stored in it.
My grandmother's recipes, along with her cast-iron skillet, went to my sister.
He lost the election along with whatever credibility he had left.
entries.русский: вместе с, наряду с — добавляет второго участника, не меняя числа подлежащего
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (a two-word preposition by strict analysis; along by itself is a preposition or a particle — along the river, bring it along)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase (an add-on), not a true clause link
entries.pattern: [X] along with [Y]. · [subject], along with [add-on], [verb agreeing with the subject alone] … · [independent clause] along with [noun phrase]. · [verb phrase] along with [-ing verb phrase].
entries.punctuation: Fence a subject add-on with commas on both sides (The pitcher, along with two coaches, was ejected); never a comma after along with itself. Those commas are punctuation only — they do not change agreement, and the verb matches the first noun with or without them. No comma when the phrase simply trails a complete clause as part of it (She brought the contract along with a check).
entries.variants: together with · in addition to · as well as · and (the true coordinator — the one addition word that does make the subject plural)
entries.see also: as well as, and, plus, not to mention, both … and

entries.meaning: Closes an open-ended list by pointing at the members not named: "more items of the same kind." It is the neutral written extender — plainer than et cetera, more respectable than and stuff — and it works only when the pattern is clear enough for a reader to continue it unaided.
examples: Bring the deed, the survey, the insurance binder, and so forth.
She handles payroll, scheduling, and so forth, while I deal with the customers.
The course covers tenses, participles, irregular verbs, and so forth.
We spent the morning on permits, inspections, and so forth, and never got to the design.
There was the usual talk about the weather, the roads, the price of feed, and so forth.
He listed every objection — cost, timing, staffing and so on and so forth — without offering a single fix.
entries.русский: и так далее, и тому подобное — нейтральный письменный способ оставить список открытым
entries.register: neutral to formal; the written counterpart of and stuff
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (a general extender — the coordinator and plus a fixed placeholder for the members not named)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase — closes a list with a vague final member; never joins finite clauses
entries.pattern: [X], [Y], and so forth. · [X], [Y], [Z], and so forth. · [list], and so forth, [rest of the clause]. · [list] and so on and so forth (emphatic doubling)
entries.punctuation: Take the comma the list would take before its final item — American editing keeps the serial comma in front of it (forms, permits, and so forth). A second comma closes it when the sentence runs on. It ends a list and never introduces one, so nothing else follows it inside the list.
entries.variants: and so on · et cetera / etc. · and the like · and so on and so forth (emphatic) · and suchlike (dated)
entries.see also: et cetera / etc., and the like / or the like, and stuff / and everything / and all that, or something, and

entries.term: and stuff / and everything / and all that
entries.meaning: The spoken general extenders: they close a list by gesturing at more of the same and signal that the speaker assumes you can fill in the rest. The three are not quite interchangeable — and everything leans toward completeness ("the whole business"), and all that toward dismissal, and and stuff is the plain all-purpose one.
examples: We got chips, salsa, and stuff for the game.
He kept apologizing, saying he'd been swamped at work and everything.
She's pleasant and all that, but I wouldn't want to work for her.
The doctor asked about diet, exercise, sleep, and all that.
I still have to pack, print the tickets, and stuff like that.
They redid the floors, repainted the kitchen, and everything — you wouldn't know it was the same house.
entries.русский: и всё такое, и всё прочее — разг., устное незавершённое перечисление
entries.register: informal; spoken, rare in edited prose except in quoted speech
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (general extenders — a reduced and plus a vague placeholder)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase — closes a list, a noun phrase, or a whole clause with a vague final member
entries.pattern: [X] and stuff. · [X], [Y], and everything. · [clause] and all that. · [X] and stuff like that. · [X] and all that jazz.
entries.punctuation: No comma before it in speech-like writing, where it runs on as part of the last item (chips and salsa and stuff); use one only if the list already carries serial commas. Never a comma after it. Outside dialogue, editing usually cuts it or swaps in and so on.
entries.variants: and stuff like that · and things · and all · and whatnot · and all that jazz · and so on (neutral) · and so forth (formal)
entries.see also: and so forth, or something, and the like / or the like, et cetera / etc., and

entries.term: and the like / or the like
entries.meaning: Extends a list to cover things of the same kind, and it is the extender a contract or a manual reaches for, because "of the same kind" is a slightly tighter promise than et cetera makes. Use the or form when only one example has been given, or when the list offers alternatives rather than an inventory.
examples: Bring a passport, a birth certificate, or the like.
The lease forbids grills, space heaters, and the like on the balcony.
Damage from earthquake, flood, and the like is excluded from the policy.
He collects stamps, coins, old survey maps, and the like.
Use a level, a plumb bob, or the like to check that the frame is true.
The store sells tents, sleeping bags, camp stoves, and the like, but nothing for climbing.
entries.русский: и тому подобное — вещи того же рода; книжн., техн. и юр. проза
entries.register: neutral to formal; at home in technical, legal, and administrative prose
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (a general extender)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase — closes a list with a vague final member; never joins finite clauses
entries.pattern: [X], [Y], and the like. · [X] or the like. · [list], and the like, [rest of the clause]. · [single example] or the like.
entries.punctuation: Comma before it in a serial list — the same comma the final item would take — and a second comma when the sentence continues. No comma after it. Pick and the like after a positive inventory and or the like after a single example or a negative.
entries.variants: and suchlike (dated) · and similar · or similar · and so forth · et cetera · and the rest (rhetorical)
entries.see also: and so forth, et cetera / etc., and stuff / and everything / and all that, as well as, or

entries.meaning: Says that the figure just named is, if anything, an understatement — "that much, plus an unspecified extra." It always follows the quantity it inflates and can never introduce anything, which is what separates it from the sequential and then it grew out of.
examples: The repair cost us the whole deposit, and then some.
She works forty hours a week, and then some.
That truck will haul a ton, and then some.
"Was it worth the drive?" "And then some."
He paid back every dollar he owed me, and then some.
The renovation ate up our summer, and then some.
entries.русский: и даже больше, и с лихвой — разг.: названная величина ещё занижена
entries.register: informal; conversational, and common in sports and feature writing
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (a fixed additive tag; distinct from the ordinary sequence and then + some)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase — a clause-final tag that outbids the amount just stated
entries.pattern: [clause naming a quantity], and then some. · [X], and then some. · And then some. (standing alone as a reply)
entries.punctuation: Comma before and then some when it caps a full clause; no comma inside it, and none after it, since it ends the sentence. As a standalone reply it takes a period of its own.
entries.variants: and more · and some (regional) · if not more · and change (with money and time: two hours and change)
entries.see also: and then, if not, plus, not to mention, and

entries.meaning: An older additive that tacks a second item onto the first without disturbing the subject, exactly as as well as does today. Editors of nineteenth-century texts and drafters of old-style deeds still meet it; nobody says it.
examples: The estate passed to his widow, as also the lands in Cheshire.
The volume prints the sermons, as also the letters of 1842.
We are bound by the treaty, as also by the custom of the port.
The catalogue lists the coins, as also the medals struck for the coronation.
She had charge of the household accounts, as also of the tenants' rents.
The rule binds the executor, as also any successor in the office.
entries.русский: а также — устар., книжн.: старинный аналог as well as
entries.register: archaic, formal; scholarly editions, old-style legal recitals, and devotional prose
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (archaic; a fossilized additive, close kin to as well as)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase (an add-on) — joins noun phrases and prepositional phrases; not a finite-clause link
entries.pattern: [X], as also [Y]. · [independent clause], as also [noun phrase]. · [list], as also [final add-on]. · [prepositional phrase], as also [matching prepositional phrase].
entries.punctuation: Comma before as also, none after it. Treat it as period costume in present-day American prose: outside legal recitals, editions of older texts, and deliberate pastiche, write as well as or and also.
entries.variants: as well as (the living equivalent) · and also · as likewise (rarer) · together with
entries.see also: as well as, along with, in conjunction with, yea, likewise

entries.meaning: Spells out the alternative being ruled out, and spells it out deliberately — it is what a writer reaches for when the rejected option has to go on the record. Two limits separate it from rather than: it cannot take a bare infinitive (I'd walk rather than pay, never as opposed to pay), and it never joins finite clauses. Where versus frames a contest between two things, as opposed to heads off a misreading of one of them.
examples: We're talking about a loan, as opposed to a grant.
The study measured hours actually worked as opposed to hours billed.
As opposed to the old model, this one holds a charge for a full day.
Renting, as opposed to buying, keeps our options open for another year.
I asked for a direct flight as opposed to whatever the site found cheapest.
The complaint names the parent company as opposed to the local franchise.
entries.русский: в отличие от, а не — прямо называет отвергаемую альтернативу
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (a three-word preposition by strict analysis; elsewhere opposed is the past participle of the verb oppose — she opposed the merger)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase of contrast — joins noun phrases, -ing clauses, and adjective phrases; never finite clauses
entries.pattern: [X] as opposed to [Y]. · [independent clause], as opposed to [noun phrase]. · [-ing form] as opposed to [-ing form]. · [subject], as opposed to [rejected alternative], [verb] … · As opposed to [X], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma when it joins two parallel words or phrases (a loan as opposed to a grant). Comma before it when the contrast is tacked onto a finished clause, and a comma on each side when it interrupts. A fronted As opposed to phrase takes a comma after the phrase. Never a comma after to.
entries.variants: rather than · instead of · and not · versus (shorter, and the usual choice in headings and tables)
entries.see also: rather than, versus, but rather, or, whereas

entries.meaning: Tacks one more item onto what has just been said and marks it as more of the same: "that too." American English mostly says too in this slot and keeps as well for writing and for a slightly more measured tone; also does the same work but sits before the verb rather than at the end. Do not confuse it with the coordinator as well as, which stands between the two items it joins instead of trailing them.
examples: The ticket covers the museum, and the sculpture garden as well.
She speaks Portuguese, and a little Italian as well.
We'll need a permit, and probably an inspection as well.
If you're going up to the counter, get me a coffee as well.
He lost the house and, in the end, the business as well.
The clinic is open Saturdays, and two evenings a week as well.
entries.русский: тоже, также — в конце фразы; в амер. речи обычно говорят too
entries.register: neutral; a shade more formal than too in American speech, and the ordinary everyday form in British and Canadian English
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (an additive adverb by strict analysis — the clause-final counterpart of also and too; distinct from the coordinator as well as and from the manner adverbial as well, "equally skillfully")
entries.clause type: coordinate tag — adds the phrase or clause it ends to what came before; never links two clauses itself
entries.pattern: [clause] as well. · [subject] [verb] [X] as well. · [clause], and [second item] as well. · As well, [clause]. (sentence-initial; chiefly Canadian and business writing, and disliked by American editors)
entries.punctuation: No comma before clause-final as well — it belongs to the clause it ends (She's coming as well); add one only to mark it as an afterthought (and the garden, as well). Nothing follows it, since it closes the sentence. It cannot join two independent clauses on its own: He was tired, as well he was hungry is impossible — write and he was hungry as well, or start a new sentence.
entries.variants: too (the ordinary American clause-final form) · also (usually before the verb) · besides · to boot (wry) · as well as (the two-word coordinator — a different item) · as well … as (correlative)
entries.see also: as well as, to boot, either, and, also, likewise

entries.meaning: Adds a second item while leaving the first one grammatically in charge, and that is the whole difference from and. A subject joined by as well as stays singular (The coach, as well as the players, was fined), and a verb after it takes the -ing form (She writes the newsletter as well as running the website). Watch the ambiguity built into the phrase: He speaks Portuguese as well as Spanish can mean "in addition to Spanish" (the conjunction) or "as fluently as he speaks Spanish" (the comparative). Only context, a comma, or a rewrite settles it.
examples: The manager, as well as the interns, was invited to the retirement lunch.
The tuition covers books as well as lab fees.
She writes the newsletter as well as running the website.
The storm knocked out power in Dayton as well as three counties to the south.
The clinic is open Saturdays as well as weekday evenings.
The report criticizes the contractor, as well as the agency that hired him.
entries.русский: а также, равно как и — добавляет второе, не делая подлежащее множественным
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (identical in form to the comparative as … as wrapped around the adverb well: She plays as well as her brother)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase (an add-on), not a true clause link
entries.pattern: [X] as well as [Y]. · [subject], as well as [add-on], [singular verb] … · [verb phrase] as well as [-ing verb phrase].
entries.punctuation: When the phrase is a parenthetical add-on to the subject, fence it with commas on both sides (The manager, as well as the interns, was invited). Without the commas it is open to being read as the comparative as well as — but the commas change nothing grammatically: the verb agrees with the first noun either way. Never a comma after as well as itself.
entries.variants: along with · together with · in addition to — all three behave the same way for agreement
entries.see also: along with, and, plus, not to mention, both … and

entries.meaning: Adds a second item and claims it outranks the first on the very scale the first was measured by: better yet upgrades, worse yet piles on. That ranking is what separates it from the neutral add-ons — not to mention adds without ordering, and and then some inflates a quantity rather than naming a new item. After or it withdraws the first option instead of adding to it (Email it, or better yet, bring a copy).
examples: The apartment is cheap; better yet, it's two blocks from the train.
Email me the file, or better yet, bring a printed copy.
We could meet Thursday — better yet, let's just do it over lunch.
Better yet, the whole thing runs on batteries you already own.
The flight was four hours late; worse yet, they lost both our bags.
He forgot the tickets, and worse yet, he'd left his wallet on the counter.
The roof leaks and the furnace is shot; worse yet, the seller won't come down a dollar.
entries.русский: а ещё лучше — второй вариант, превосходящий первый по той же шкале
entries.register: neutral; conversational, and common in journalism, reviews, and sales copy
entries.type: conjunctive adverb (a fixed comparative escalator, reduced from and what is better yet; the negative twin worse yet behaves identically)
entries.clause type: discourse connective — heads a clause that outbids the one before it on the same scale
entries.pattern: [clause]; better yet, [stronger clause]. · [clause]. Better yet, [clause]. · [X], or better yet, [better X]. · [clause], and worse yet, [worse clause]. · Worse yet, [clause]. (sentence-initial)
entries.punctuation: It is an adverb, not a coordinator, so between two independent clauses it needs a semicolon or a period in front of it (The place is cheap; better yet, it's two blocks from the train) — a comma alone there is a comma splice. A comma follows it in every position. When and or or does the joining, the phrase turns parenthetical and takes a comma on each side (and, better yet, the parking is free).
entries.variants: worse yet (the negative twin) · better still / worse still (a shade more formal) · even better / even worse · or better yet (offering a replacement rather than an addition) · what's better / what's worse
entries.see also: on top of that, not only that, not to mention, and then some, if not, moreover

entries.meaning: Adds a second factor and presents the two as working together to produce one effect, which is what sets it apart from the neutral add-ons: coupled with is nearly always causal. The subject stays singular — Poor pay, coupled with long hours, drives people out.
examples: The drought, coupled with the new tariffs, wiped out the family's margin.
Poor pay coupled with long hours drives young teachers out of the profession.
Coupled with a mild winter, the early thaw brought the river up two weeks ahead of schedule.
Her years abroad, coupled with fluent Portuguese, made her the obvious hire.
The medication, coupled with physical therapy, restored most of his range of motion.
Slow sales coupled with rising rent forced the shop to close in March.
entries.русский: в сочетании с, вкупе с — книжн.: два фактора вместе дают один результат
entries.register: neutral to formal; business, medical, and news writing
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (a participial preposition by strict analysis, from the verb couple)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase (an add-on) — joins noun phrases and -ing clauses; never finite clauses
entries.pattern: [X] coupled with [Y] [verb agreeing with X alone] … · [subject], coupled with [add-on], [verb] … · Coupled with [X], [main clause]. · [independent clause], coupled with [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: Fence it with commas on both sides when it interrupts the subject (The drought, coupled with the tariffs, ruined him); a fronted Coupled with phrase takes a comma after the phrase. Never a comma after with. Like along with and as well as, it leaves agreement with the first noun, and the commas change nothing about that.
entries.variants: combined with · together with · along with · paired with · in combination with (formal)
entries.see also: along with, in conjunction with, in tandem with, as well as, plus

entries.meaning: Fuses two descriptions of one and the same thing, so that neither label is complete on its own: a kitchen-cum-dining room is one room doing two jobs, not two rooms. It stays bookish or faintly jokey in American English, where writer/director and plain and do the work; the spelling also coincides with an unrelated vulgar slang noun, which is one more reason American writers avoid it.
examples: They rent a kitchen-cum-dining room at the back of the flat.
He works as a driver-cum-bodyguard for the family.
The place is a bar-cum-bookshop that closes whenever the owner feels like it.
She is the founder-cum-chief-engineer of the whole operation.
The building started life as a chapel-cum-schoolhouse for the mill workers.
What we got was a lecture-cum-sales-pitch that ran ninety minutes.
entries.русский: он же, совмещённый с — книжн./шутл.: kitchen-cum-dining room — кухня-столовая
entries.register: formal or jocular; chiefly British, and uncommon in American writing
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (the Latin preposition cum "with", used in English to fuse two nouns into one compound)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase — joins two nouns naming one thing; never clauses
entries.pattern: [noun]-cum-[noun] · [role]-cum-[second role] · [noun] cum [noun] (older, unhyphenated)
entries.punctuation: Hyphenate it to both nouns and put no spaces or commas around it (a kitchen-cum-dining room). The whole compound behaves as a single noun and takes a singular verb. Older and more formal writing sometimes drops the hyphens; American editing usually rewrites with and or with a slash.
entries.variants: unhyphenated cum · and · / (writer/director) · slash (a bar slash bookshop — informal spoken)
entries.see also: and, and/or, plus, versus, as well as

entries.meaning: The negative twin of too: it says that a negative already stated holds for one more person or case. Swap in too and the sentence breaks (I don't like it too), which is the quickest test for it. Where nor carries its own negation and forces inversion, bare either leaves the second clause's own not in place and adds nothing but "likewise."
examples: I don't like horror movies, and my sister doesn't either.
He never wrote back, and he didn't call either.
"I can't make Thursday." "I can't either."
The store doesn't take checks, and it doesn't take cards either.
She wasn't rude, exactly, but she wasn't friendly either.
If you're not going, I'm not going either.
entries.русский: тоже не — отрицательный двойник too: I don't like it either «мне тоже не нравится»
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (an additive adverb by strict analysis — the negative-polarity counterpart of too and as well; distinct from the correlative either … or and from the determiner and pronoun either, as in either road will get you there)
entries.clause type: coordinate tag — attaches one more negative to a negative already on the table; never links two clauses itself
entries.pattern: [negative clause] either. · [subject] [negative verb] [X] either. · [negative clause], and [second negative clause] either. · not [X] either · compare positive [clause] too.
entries.punctuation: No comma before clause-final either in ordinary use (I don't like it either); a comma marks it as an afterthought (and she never called, either), and American editing allows both. Nothing follows it. It cannot join two clauses by itself — He didn't call, either he wrote is impossible; use and … either, or nor with inversion.
entries.variants: too / as well (the positive-polarity forms) · neither with inversion (neither do I) · me either (spoken) · correlative either … or and determiner either (either road) are different words
entries.see also: neither, nor, as well, either … or, also

entries.meaning: The bare conjunction else meaning "otherwise" survives in proverbs, hymn and scripture texts, and deliberately old-sounding prose; everyday American English requires or in front of it. The living, ordinary else is an adverb attached to an indefinite word (somewhere else, what else), not a conjunction at all.
examples: Speak now, else forever hold your peace.
We must act tonight, else the chance is gone.
Take the earlier flight, else you'll be stuck in that airport until midnight.
He must have known, else why keep the letters all these years?
Write the address down, else you'll be circling that block for an hour.
Say nothing of this to your brother, else the whole family hears about it by Sunday.
entries.русский: иначе, а не то — устар. как самостоятельный союз; живёт в основном в or else
entries.register: literary, archaic on its own; neutral inside or else
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (bare use); adverb when attached to an indefinite word
entries.clause type: coordinate clause of alternative consequence
entries.pattern: [independent clause], else [independent clause]. (literary) · [imperative], else [consequence]. · [clause], else why [auxiliary] [subject] [rest]? (surviving idiom) — modern American prose writes or else in all three slots
entries.punctuation: Comma before conjunctive else. In present-day American prose, write or else instead; bare else in this slot reads as period costume.
entries.variants: or else · otherwise · adverbial else after an indefinite (something else, who else) is a different word class
entries.see also: or else, or, otherwise, unless

entries.ipa: /ɛt ˈsɛtərə/, often /ɛt ˈsɛtrə/; /ɛk ˈsɛtərə/ is widely heard and widely condemned
entries.meaning: The Latin general extender: "and the other things of this sort." It is the standard written way to leave a list open, but it earns its keep only when the reader can actually continue the pattern — after two vague items it says nothing, which is why editors often cut it and name one more item instead.
examples: Bring pens, paper, tape, etc.
The kit holds bandages, antiseptic, tweezers, etc., but no scissors.
The form asks for name, address, date of birth, et cetera.
He gave me the whole speech about deadlines and professionalism, etc., etc.
Charges for parking, cleaning, late checkout, etc. are listed on the back of the folio.
We covered the usual ground — budget, staffing, timelines, etc. — in about an hour.
entries.русский: и так далее, и прочее — лат. сокращение, оставляющее список открытым
entries.register: neutral; etc. belongs to writing, the spelled-out form to formal or ironic use
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (a general extender borrowed whole from Latin et cetera "and the rest"; etc. is its abbreviation)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase — closes a list with a vague final member; never joins clauses
entries.pattern: [X], [Y], etc. · [X], [Y], etc., [rest of the clause]. · [list], et cetera. · [list], etc., etc. (emphatic doubling)
entries.punctuation: Keep the period on etc., and take a comma before it in a serial list (pens, paper, etc.). When the sentence continues, a comma follows the abbreviation's period; when the sentence ends there, that one period does both jobs — never type two. Never write and etc., since et already means "and," and never pair it with such as or for example, which have already marked the list as partial.
entries.variants: etc. · &c. (older) · et al. (of people, not things) · and so forth · and so on · and the like
entries.see also: and so forth, and the like / or the like, and stuff / and everything / and all that, and, inter alia

entries.meaning: Reaches past the item just named to a stronger one and floats it without quite asserting it — "X, and possibly more than X." It is the upward mirror of let alone and much less: those two run down a scale from a stated negative, while if not runs up from a stated positive and needs no negative in front of it at all. The hedge is real and worth respecting — a reporter who writes hundreds, if not thousands has committed to hundreds and merely raised the possibility of thousands.
examples: The repair will take weeks, if not months.
It's a difficult, if not impossible, thing to prove.
Hundreds of homes, if not thousands, lost power overnight.
He's the best shortstop in the division, if not the league.
She was annoyed, if not furious, by the time we finally showed up.
The policy is unwise, if not actually illegal.
entries.русский: если не сказать, а то и — осторожный шаг вверх: «X, а возможно, и больше»
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (scalar; distinct from the conditional if not that stands alone — If not, we'll reschedule — and from if + not inside a clause: if he's not there by six)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase, scalar — the second element is a fragment that outbids the first
entries.pattern: [X], if not [stronger X]. · [adjective], if not [stronger adjective]. · [quantity], if not [larger quantity]. · [determiner] [adjective], if not [stronger adjective], [noun] (interrupting) · [independent clause], if not [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: Comma before if not, no comma after it. When it interrupts instead of closing the sentence, fence it with a comma on each side (a difficult, if not impossible, fix). What follows is a fragment parallel to the element it outbids — never a clause with its own subject and tensed verb. Keep it apart from the conditional if not that stands as its own clause (If not, call me), which takes its comma after, not before.
entries.variants: not to say (formal) · or even · perhaps even · conditional if not (If not, we'll try Thursday) is a different construction
entries.see also: let alone, much less, not to mention, rather than, or

entries.meaning: Adds a second party or a second instrument and says the two are meant to act together — the difference between it and the merely additive along with. It is institutional language, at home in press releases, protocols, and instructions for use; in ordinary prose plain with says the same thing in one word.
examples: The university, in conjunction with two teaching hospitals, is running the trial.
This medication should be taken in conjunction with food.
The exhibit was organized in conjunction with the state historical society.
Read the manual in conjunction with the wiring diagram on the last page.
The city, in conjunction with the county, will pay for the new interchange.
The scholarship is awarded in conjunction with a summer research placement.
entries.русский: совместно с, в сочетании с — офиц.: двое действуют заодно
entries.register: formal; administrative, technical, and institutional writing
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (a complex preposition built on the noun conjunction)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase (an add-on) — joins noun phrases and -ing clauses; never finite clauses
entries.pattern: [X] in conjunction with [Y]. · [subject], in conjunction with [add-on], [verb agreeing with the subject alone] … · [verb phrase] in conjunction with [noun phrase]. · In conjunction with [X], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Fence a subject add-on with commas on both sides, and put a comma after a fronted In conjunction with phrase. Never a comma after with. Agreement stays with the first noun: The university, in conjunction with two hospitals, is running the trial.
entries.variants: in collaboration with · in partnership with · jointly with · together with · along with · with (the plain rewrite)
entries.see also: in tandem with, coupled with, along with, as well as, as also

entries.meaning: Joins two parties or two processes and insists that they move together — at the same time, at the same rate, or as a matched pair. Where along with merely adds a second item, in tandem with claims coordination in the everyday sense of the word.
examples: The fire department worked in tandem with the sheriff's office all night.
Rents have climbed in tandem with home prices for three straight years.
The new software runs in tandem with the old system until the spring.
She develops the curriculum in tandem with the teachers who will actually use it.
The city's own plan, in tandem with a federal grant, finally paid for the levee.
Two pumps operate in tandem, so one can be serviced without shutting the plant down.
entries.русский: в связке с, параллельно с — двое движутся одновременно и согласованно
entries.register: neutral to formal; business, engineering, and news writing
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (a complex preposition; tandem is a hitch with one horse behind the other)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase (an add-on) — joins noun phrases and -ing clauses; never finite clauses
entries.pattern: [X] in tandem with [Y]. · [subject], in tandem with [add-on], [verb agreeing with the subject alone] … · [verb phrase] in tandem with [noun phrase]. · [plural subject] [verb] in tandem. (bare adverbial, no with)
entries.punctuation: Commas on both sides when it interrupts the subject, none after with; agreement stays with the first noun. The bare adverbial in tandem takes no punctuation at all (The two systems run in tandem).
entries.variants: in tandem (bare adverbial) · in step with · in parallel with · side by side with · in conjunction with · together with
entries.see also: in conjunction with, coupled with, along with, as well as, plus

entries.meaning: Adds a second, more extreme item and says that if the first is already out of reach, the second is far more so. It needs a negative, a question, or some other downward-entailing context in front of it — He can cook, let alone boil water is ungrammatical, because the scale runs backward.
examples: He can't boil water, let alone cook a turkey.
I've never been to Canada, let alone Japan.
We couldn't afford the rent, let alone a second car.
She barely has time to eat, let alone train for a marathon.
Nobody remembered his birthday, let alone bought him anything.
There isn't room for a table in here — let alone a couch.
entries.русский: не говоря уже о, тем более — после отрицания: первое невозможно, второе и подавно
entries.register: neutral; conversational
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (distinct from the literal verb phrase let alone = "leave undisturbed")
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase, scalar — the second element is a fragment
entries.pattern: [negative clause], let alone [noun phrase]. · [negative clause], let alone [verb phrase matching the one before it]. · [clause with barely, hardly, or too], let alone [stronger element]. · [question], let alone [harder case]?
entries.punctuation: Comma before let alone, no comma after it; a dash in place of the comma marks a bigger jump. What follows is a fragment parallel to the constituent it echoes — a noun phrase (let alone Japan), a verb phrase (let alone bought him anything), a prepositional phrase — never a clause with a subject and a tensed verb of its own.
entries.variants: much less · never mind · to say nothing of (formal) · still less (formal)
entries.see also: much less, still less, never mind, not to mention, if not, nor

entries.meaning: Subtracts the second item from the first, and the whole phrase stays singular — Ten minus three is seven, not are. In casual use it means "and without," usually with a wry note: He showed up minus the beard. It is grouped with the coordinators here because it patterns exactly against plus, though grammars class the "without" use as a preposition.
examples: Nine minus four is five.
The payment is your salary minus taxes and insurance.
He came back from the trip minus one suitcase.
We got the whole crew, minus the two who had a wedding that weekend.
That's the same recipe minus the anchovies.
The final total, minus shipping, came to eighty dollars.
entries.русский: минус; без — арифметическое вычитание; разг. «без чего-то»: явился без бороды
entries.register: neutral in arithmetic; informal and wry in the "without" sense
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (a preposition by strict analysis in the "without" sense; also a noun and an adjective — a minus sign, a B minus)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase — joins noun phrases only, never finite clauses
entries.pattern: [number] minus [number] [singular verb] [number]. · [noun phrase] minus [noun phrase]. · [independent clause] minus [noun phrase]. · [subject], minus [noun phrase], [verb] … (parenthetical)
entries.punctuation: No commas in arithmetic (Nine minus four is five). In the "without" sense the comma before minus is optional and depends on how parenthetical the phrase feels; never a comma after it.
entries.variants: less (the price less tax) · without · sans (jocular)
entries.see also: plus, times, versus, as well as

entries.meaning: Does the same job as let alone — naming a bigger case that follows automatically from a negative already stated — but reads a shade more formal and turns up more often in writing than in speech. Like let alone, it is ungrammatical after a positive clause.
examples: She doesn't have a bicycle, much less a car.
Most of us can't name our senators, much less our state representatives.
He never apologized, much less offered to fix it.
The town couldn't fund a library, much less a new school.
I wouldn't lend him a pen, much less five hundred dollars.
There's no proof he was there, much less that he took anything.
entries.русский: тем более не, не говоря уже о — то же, что let alone, но чуть книжнее
entries.register: neutral; a shade more formal than let alone
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (distinct from the literal comparative much less: much less money)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase, scalar — the second element is a fragment
entries.pattern: [negative clause], much less [noun phrase]. · [negative clause], much less [verb phrase matching the one before it]. · [negative clause ending in a content noun], much less that [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma before much less, no comma after it. What follows is a fragment parallel to the constituent it echoes — a noun phrase (much less a car), a verb phrase (much less offered to fix it), or a that-clause when the first half already ends in one (no proof he was there, much less that he took anything) — but never a free-standing clause with its own subject.
entries.variants: let alone · still less (formal) · never mind (informal)
entries.see also: let alone, never mind, still less, not to mention, nor

entries.meaning: The negative echo: it picks up a negative just stated and extends it to a second party. Standard American English requires subject–auxiliary inversion after it, and that is exactly what separates it from either — Neither did I and I didn't either say the same thing, but neither pattern tolerates the other's word order. An American meets the uninverted, clause-final neither in regional speech and in novelists writing dialect, not in edited prose, where either fills that slot.
examples: I couldn't sleep, and neither could she.
"I've never seen it." "Neither have I."
The heat didn't work. Neither did the hot water.
He wasn't invited, and neither was his brother.
"I don't want to go." "Me neither."
The lease says nothing about pets; neither does it mention the parking space.
"I ain't got no money, and she ain't got none neither," he told the deputy. (dialect — edited English writes either here)
entries.русский: и я тоже нет — подхватывает отрицание; требует инверсии: Neither do I
entries.register: neutral in the inverted form (Neither do I) and in spoken me neither; nonstandard clause-final (I don't like it neither), where it belongs to Southern, Appalachian, and other regional speech and to stage dialect in fiction
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (an additive negative adverb by strict analysis, taking subject–auxiliary inversion; distinct from the correlative neither … nor and from the determiner and pronoun neither, as in neither road was plowed)
entries.clause type: inverted echo clause — repeats a negative already stated and applies it to someone or something else
entries.pattern: [negative clause]. Neither [auxiliary or be] [subject]. · [negative clause], and neither [auxiliary] [subject]. · [negative clause]; neither [auxiliary] [subject] [rest]. · Me neither. (spoken short answer) · nonstandard [negative clause] neither. (clause-final, dialectal)
entries.punctuation: Comma before neither when and joins the two clauses (I couldn't sleep, and neither could she). Standing on its own it needs a period or a semicolon in front of it and never a bare comma: I didn't know, neither did anyone else is a comma splice — write I didn't know. Neither did anyone else. The inversion is obligatory (neither did she, never neither she did), and Me neither takes no internal punctuation.
entries.variants: either (the standard uninverted, clause-final form) · nor (same inversion, but it joins rather than answers) · me neither / me either (spoken) · neither … nor (correlative) · clause-final neither (I don't neither) is dialectal, not standard
entries.see also: either, nor, nor yet, neither … nor, likewise

entries.meaning: The most casual member of the let alone family: it names a bigger case and points out that the first one already rules it out. Like let alone and much less it needs a negative or some other downward-entailing context ahead of it, and unlike them it almost never survives into edited writing. Keep it apart from the imperative never mind meaning "forget it," which takes an object and stands on its own.
examples: He can't manage a two-week trip, never mind a year abroad.
I haven't finished the first chapter, never mind the whole book.
The kids can barely sit through a cartoon, never mind a three-hour opera.
We couldn't get a table on a Tuesday, never mind a Saturday night.
She's never driven a stick shift, never mind hauled a trailer.
There's no money for raises this year — never mind bonuses.
entries.русский: уж куда там, не говоря уже о — разг.: самый просторечный из ряда let alone
entries.register: informal; conversational, rare in edited prose
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (also an ordinary imperative verb phrase: Never mind the mess)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase, scalar — the second element is a fragment
entries.pattern: [negative clause], never mind [noun phrase]. · [negative clause], never mind [verb phrase matching the one before it]. · [clause with barely or hardly], never mind [harder case].
entries.punctuation: Comma before never mind, no comma after it; a dash in place of the comma marks a bigger jump. What follows is a fragment parallel to the constituent it echoes, never a clause with its own subject.
entries.variants: let alone (neutral) · much less · still less (formal) · to say nothing of (formal) · imperative never mind (Never mind, I'll do it myself) is a different construction
entries.see also: let alone, much less, still less, not to mention, to say nothing of

entries.meaning: Announces that what was just said is not the whole of it and that something further, usually worse, is coming. It differs from the correlative it grew out of in needing no second half in the same sentence: not only … but also balances two elements inside one clause, while not only that points backward across a full stop.
examples: He showed up two hours late. Not only that, he brought three friends.
The bill doubled; not only that, they charged us for a room we never used.
She runs the shop alone. Not only that, she keeps the books herself.
The road is closed all summer — not only that, the detour adds forty minutes.
Not only that, but the warranty had expired the week before it broke.
They never apologized. Not only that, they sent a second invoice.
entries.русский: мало того, и это ещё не всё — отсылает назад, через точку, к сказанному
entries.register: neutral; conversational, and common in opinion writing and complaint
entries.type: conjunctive adverb (a fixed clausal connective, the free-standing descendant of the correlative not only … but also; distinct from not only heading a that-clause, as in not only that he lied, but that he kept lying)
entries.clause type: discourse connective — heads a new clause that adds a further, usually stronger item
entries.pattern: [clause]. Not only that, [clause]. · [clause]; not only that, [clause]. · [clause]. Not only that, but [clause]. · [clause] — not only that, [clause]. · Not only that, but [clause] as well.
entries.punctuation: Put a period or a semicolon in front of it when two independent clauses are involved (He was late; not only that, he was rude) — a comma there is a comma splice, since the phrase is an adverbial and not a coordinator. A comma always follows it. The but that so often trails it is optional and takes no comma of its own.
entries.variants: not only that, but … · and not only that · what's more · on top of that · moreover (formal) · correlative not only … but also
entries.see also: on top of that, better yet, not to mention, to boot, not only … but also, moreover

entries.meaning: Adds a further item while pretending to leave it out — a rhetorical move that presents the addition as too obvious to need saying. Unlike let alone and much less, it needs no negative in front of it and does not rank the two items on a scale.
examples: The trip cost us two weeks of vacation, not to mention four thousand dollars.
He's late every morning, not to mention rude about it.
Rewiring the house would take a month, not to mention an electrician we can't afford.
The noise was unbearable, not to mention the dust.
She runs the whole department, not to mention two committees.
That neighborhood has better schools, not to mention a grocery store you can walk to.
entries.русский: не говоря уже о — добавляет пункт под видом умолчания; отрицание не нужно
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (distinct from the literal infinitive not to mention: He promised not to mention the money)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase (an add-on)
entries.pattern: [X], not to mention [Y]. · [independent clause], not to mention [noun phrase]. · [independent clause], not to mention [adjective phrase or verb phrase matching the one before it].
entries.punctuation: Comma before not to mention, no comma after it. Dashes or parentheses work better when the add-on runs long.
entries.variants: to say nothing of (formal) · never mind · plus (informal) · let alone (only after a negative)
entries.see also: to say nothing of, let alone, much less, never mind, plus, as well as

entries.ipa: /ˌɑn ˈtɑp əv ˌðæt/, weak /ˌɑn ˈtɑp ə ˌðæt/
entries.meaning: Piles one more item onto a load the reader is already meant to feel, which is why it leans negative: on top of that almost always adds a further cost, delay, or insult. In addition and besides carry no such freight, and over and above — the same metaphor in formal dress — stacks amounts rather than grievances.
examples: The flight was canceled. On top of that, the hotel gave away our room.
Tuition went up nine percent; on top of that, they cut the shuttle to campus.
She works two jobs, and on top of that, she's finishing her degree at night.
The repair ran four hundred dollars — on top of that, we lost a day of work.
On top of everything else, the dog got into the trash.
He never returned the ladder, and on top of that, he broke it.
entries.русский: вдобавок ко всему, и в довершение — разг., почти всегда о новой неприятности
entries.register: informal to neutral; conversational, and at home in feature writing and complaint rather than in contracts, where over and above does the same work
entries.type: conjunctive adverb (a fixed prepositional connective; distinct from the literal spatial on top of that — the box on top of that one — and from additive on top of + noun phrase, a surcharge on top of the fare)
entries.clause type: discourse connective — heads a clause that adds one more item to a list already felt to be heavy
entries.pattern: [clause]. On top of that, [clause]. · [clause]; on top of that, [clause]. · [clause], and on top of that, [clause]. · On top of everything else, [clause]. · compare prepositional on top of [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it between two independent clauses (Tuition went up; on top of that, they cut the shuttle) — a comma there is a comma splice, unless and is doing the joining, in which case the phrase turns parenthetical and takes a comma on each side (and, on top of that, the car wouldn't start). A comma follows it. The prepositional use needs no comma at all.
entries.variants: on top of everything else · on top of it all · besides that · what's more · in addition (formal) · over and above (formal, and of amounts rather than grievances) · prepositional on top of + noun phrase
entries.see also: over and above, not only that, not to mention, to boot, plus, besides, in addition

entries.meaning: Introduces the single thing that spoils or qualifies what was just said — "but there's a catch." It is squarely conversational; in edited prose the same job goes to but or except that.
examples: I'd love to come, only I have a deadline Friday.
It's a great apartment, only the radiators bang all night.
We'd have made it on time, only the tunnel was closed.
She'd tell you herself, only she's not speaking to either of us.
I would have called. Only it was two in the morning.
The car runs fine, only it burns oil.
entries.русский: только вот, вот только — разг.: оговорка, портящая всё только что сказанное
entries.register: informal; conversational
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (far more often a focusing adverb or an adjective)
entries.clause type: coordinate clause, adversative — equivalent to but or except that
entries.pattern: [independent clause], only [independent clause]. · Only [clause]. (as a following sentence, informal)
entries.punctuation: Comma before conjunctive only. Without that comma the word is read as the focusing adverb, which attaches to whatever follows it and changes the meaning of the sentence.
entries.variants: except that · but (the neutral equivalents) · adverbial only (I only asked) is a different word class
entries.see also: but, but then, except that, however

entries.meaning: Marks the item just named as approximate: the speaker is not sure of it and does not want to be held to it. After a negative it switches to or anything (He didn't apologize or anything), and in a question it turns aggressive — Are you deaf or something?
examples: He's a second cousin or something — I've never been clear on it.
She said she'd be here at seven or something like that.
Grab a sandwich or something on the way over.
Are you trying to get us both fired or something?
They never called, never wrote, never sent a card or anything.
It cost eighty dollars or something, which seemed like a lot at the time.
entries.русский: или что-то в этом роде — разг.: говорящий не ручается за точность
entries.register: informal; spoken
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (a general extender — or plus a vague placeholder)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase — a hedging tag that closes a noun phrase, a clause, or a guess
entries.pattern: [X] or something. · [clause] or something. · [X] or something like that. · [negative clause] or anything. · Are you [adjective] or something? (challenge)
entries.punctuation: No comma before it — it belongs to the phrase it trails. A comma follows only when the sentence keeps going (He's a cousin or something, I think). Never a comma between the two words.
entries.variants: or something like that · or whatever · or anything (after a negative) · or so (with quantities) · or some such (formal)
entries.see also: or what, and stuff / and everything / and all that, and so forth, et cetera / etc., or

entries.meaning: Closes a question with a shrug at the alternatives it declines to name, and it does one of two jobs. After a description it demands agreement (Is that a view, or what?); after a plain yes-or-no question it demands a decision (Are we ordering, or what?). Both are conversational, and neither survives into edited prose.
examples: Is that a view, or what?
Are we ordering, or what?
Was that the best game you've seen all year, or what?
So is he coming to the wedding, or what?
Did they forget about us entirely, or what?
Is this kid a natural, or what?
entries.русский: или как? ну разве не...? — разг. концовка вопроса: требует согласия или решения
entries.register: informal; spoken
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (a fixed tag — or plus the interrogative what)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase — a clause-final tag, and only in questions
entries.pattern: Is [subject] [adjective], or what? (rhetorical — "obviously yes") · Are [subject] [verb]-ing, or what? (impatient — "decide") · [yes-or-no question], or what?
entries.punctuation: Comma before or what in writing, and always a question mark after it: it exists only in questions. No comma between the two words, and nothing follows it in the sentence.
entries.variants: or not? (the neutral alternative-question form) · or anything? · or something? · huh? (spoken)
entries.see also: or something, or else, or, and stuff / and everything / and all that

entries.meaning: Names the one member a statement does not cover, so it needs a negative, a universal, or a question in front of it to have something to subtract from. Other than that has hardened into a discourse formula for waving away everything already mentioned.
examples: No one other than the owner has a key.
Other than the rain on Tuesday, the whole trip went perfectly.
There's nothing on the menu other than fish.
She never discussed the case with anyone other than her attorney.
The flight sat on the tarmac for two hours; other than that, it was fine.
Any solution other than raising taxes is going to take years.
entries.русский: кроме, помимо — единственное исключение; нужны отрицание, вопрос или «все»
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (exceptive; a two-word preposition by strict analysis, built on comparative than)
