entries.clause type: coordinate phrase, exceptive — subtracts one member from the set just named; also fronts the sentence
entries.pattern: [negative or universal clause] other than [noun phrase]. · no one / nothing / nobody other than [X] · Other than [X], [main clause]. · [noun] other than [noun] (any option other than surrender) · Other than that, [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma when it attaches straight to the noun it excepts (no one other than the owner). Comma before it when it trails a finished clause, and a comma after a fronted Other than phrase (Other than the rain, the trip was perfect). Never a comma after than.
entries.variants: apart from · aside from · except / except for · besides · outside of (informal) · prepositional but (no one but the owner)
entries.see also: outside of, rather than, as opposed to, but, save

entries.meaning: The colloquial American except for: it lifts one item out of an otherwise sweeping statement. Editors object that outside is properly spatial and prefer apart from or other than in writing; in speech it is completely ordinary and completely clear.
examples: Outside of a couple of typos, the draft is clean.
Nobody knew about the offer outside of the two of us.
Outside of one summer in Maine, she has never left the state.
She hasn't taken a day off, outside of the week her mother was sick.
There's nothing to do out here outside of fishing.
The car needs tires; outside of that, it's in good shape.
entries.русский: кроме, если не считать — разг., амер.; на письме предпочитают apart from
entries.register: informal; American, and avoided in edited prose
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (exceptive; distinct from the literal spatial outside of — outside of town)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase, exceptive — subtracts one member from the set just named; also fronts the sentence
entries.pattern: Outside of [X], [main clause]. · [clause], outside of [noun phrase]. · nobody / nothing outside of [X] · Outside of that, [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted Outside of phrase; comma before it when it trails a finished clause. Never a comma after of. In the spatial sense the of is optional and usually dropped (outside the building); in this exceptive sense it is fixed.
entries.variants: apart from · aside from · other than · except for · besides · spatial outside (of) (outside of town) is a different use
entries.see also: other than, minus, as opposed to, but, except that

entries.meaning: Adds one amount to another and insists the second is extra rather than included — the phrase a contract uses so that nobody can later claim the two figures were one. Keep it apart from above and beyond, which praises effort instead of stacking quantities.
examples: The bonus is paid over and above her base salary.
Over and above the repair bill, we lost a full week of work.
Tenants pay for utilities over and above the monthly rent.
The grant covers travel over and above the tuition award.
He wants a share of the profits over and above what he has already been paid.
The storm did structural damage over and above the flooding in the basement.
entries.русский: сверх, помимо — офиц.: вторая сумма именно добавочная, а не включённая
entries.register: formal to neutral; contracts, pay talk, and official writing
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (additive; a fixed three-word preposition)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase (an add-on) — joins noun phrases; never finite clauses
entries.pattern: [X] over and above [Y]. · [independent clause], over and above [noun phrase]. · Over and above [X], [main clause]. · over and above what / whatever [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma when the phrase attaches directly to what it adds to (a bonus over and above her salary). Comma before it when it trails a finished clause, and a comma after a fronted phrase. Never a comma inside the phrase itself.
entries.variants: in addition to · on top of · besides · above and beyond (a different idiom — "more than duty required")
entries.see also: plus, as well as, along with, not to mention, in addition

entries.meaning: In arithmetic and pricing it adds one quantity to another and leaves the subject singular (Two plus two is four). In speech it doubles as an informal and that tacks on one more reason, usually the clincher — It's closer, plus the parking is free. That clause-joining use is at home in conversation and email and out of place in formal writing.
examples: Two plus two is four.
The rate is ninety dollars a night, plus tax.
It's closer to the office, plus the parking is free.
Plus, we already paid for the tickets.
I don't have the tools for it, plus I'd probably break something.
The job comes with health insurance plus three weeks of vacation.
entries.русский: плюс; да и ещё — арифметическое сложение; разг. союз «и» с добавочным доводом
entries.register: neutral in arithmetic; informal as a clause connector
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (also a noun and an adjective — that's a plus, a B plus, a plus sign)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase; also a coordinate clause in informal use
entries.pattern: [number] plus [number] [singular verb] … · [X] plus [Y]. · [independent clause], plus [independent clause]. (informal) · Plus, [clause]. (sentence-initial, informal)
entries.punctuation: No comma when plus joins two noun phrases or numbers (rent plus utilities). Comma before clause-joining plus. Sentence-initial Plus normally takes a comma after it.
entries.variants: and (the neutral equivalent) · plus that (nonstandard) · besides (conjunctive adverb)
entries.see also: and, minus, times, as well as, not to mention, besides

entries.meaning: Names the option that was not chosen. The two halves have to be the same grammatical shape, and the form after rather than copies the form before it: I'd walk rather than pay for parking (bare verb after a bare verb), but He spends evenings reading rather than watching television (-ing after -ing). Note that the American vowel in rather is the one in cat; the British /ˈrɑːðə/ is a different sound entirely.
examples: I'd walk rather than pay for parking.
Rather than argue about it, she just paid the fee.
We took the train rather than the bus.
He spends his evenings reading rather than watching television.
The change was cosmetic rather than structural.
She'd resign rather than sign off on numbers she didn't believe.
entries.русский: а не, вместо того чтобы — называет невыбранный вариант; формы по обе стороны совпадают
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (prepositional before a noun phrase; rather on its own is an adverb of degree or preference, and than elsewhere is a comparative subordinator)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase of preference; also fronts the sentence as an adverbial
entries.pattern: [X] rather than [Y]. · Rather than [X], [main clause]. · [modal + bare verb] rather than [bare verb]. · [-ing form] rather than [-ing form].
entries.punctuation: No comma when rather than joins two parallel words or phrases (Call rather than email). Comma after a fronted Rather than phrase (Rather than argue, she paid the fee), and commas on both sides when it interrupts the sentence.
entries.variants: instead of (takes a noun or an -ing form, never a bare infinitive) · as opposed to · sooner than (older)
entries.see also: but rather, or rather, as opposed to, versus, or, whereas

entries.meaning: The most formal of the scalar add-ons — the one a judge, a philosopher, or an obituarist reaches for where speech would use let alone. It behaves exactly like much less: it demands a negative or other downward-entailing context in front of it, and the item it introduces is the harder case that the stated negative already covers. In American writing it is noticeably rarer than much less and reads as deliberately elevated.
examples: The report does not establish motive, still less intent.
He had no authority to reopen the file, still less to destroy it.
Nothing in the record suggests she knew, still less that she approved.
The treaty was never ratified, still less enforced.
We cannot explain consciousness, still less reproduce it.
She rarely spoke of her childhood, still less of the years just after the war.
entries.русский: и тем более не — книжн., самый формальный из ряда let alone / much less
entries.register: formal; chiefly written
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (distinct from the literal comparative still less: still less time than before)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase, scalar — the second element is a fragment
entries.pattern: [negative clause], still less [noun phrase]. · [negative clause], still less [verb phrase matching the one before it]. · [negative clause ending in a content noun], still less that [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma before still less, no comma after it. What follows is a fragment parallel to the constituent it echoes; it never carries a subject and a tensed verb of its own.
entries.variants: much less · let alone (neutral) · never mind (informal) · to say nothing of · literal comparative still less (still less patience) is a different word class
entries.see also: much less, let alone, never mind, to say nothing of, nor

entries.meaning: Multiplies one quantity by another and, like plus and minus, leaves the resulting subject singular. It is the third member of the arithmetic set and the only one of the three with no extension into ordinary prose: plus became an informal and and minus became an informal without, but times stayed with the numbers, surviving outside them only in multiplier phrases such as three times the price.
examples: Six times seven is forty-two.
Quick — what's eight times twelve?
Anything times zero is zero.
Rent downtown runs about three times what we pay now.
Two times the recipe should feed the whole crew.
Twelve times twelve equals one hundred forty-four.
entries.русский: умножить на — арифметическое умножение: three times four «трижды четыре»
entries.register: neutral in arithmetic; the verb use is schoolroom and informal
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (arithmetic; also the plural noun times and, informally, a verb: times it by four)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase — joins numerals and quantity expressions only, never clauses
entries.pattern: [number] times [number] [singular verb] [number]. · [number] times [noun phrase]. · [indefinite pronoun] times [number] [singular verb] [number]. · What's [number] times [number]? (question)
entries.punctuation: No commas anywhere around it, and the whole phrase takes a singular verb (Six times seven is forty-two). Spell it out in running prose and use × between figures. Do not carry it over to dimensions: × between two measurements is read by, not times (an eight-by-ten print).
entries.variants: × (multiplication sign) · multiplied by (formal) · by — the word for dimensions, where times is wrong (eight by ten) · verbal times (Times that by three — informal)
entries.see also: plus, minus, versus, and

entries.meaning: Adds one final item and presents it as a bonus thrown in on top of the rest. It means roughly what as well and besides mean, but carries a wry, faintly antique tone that neither of them has, and unlike them it is locked to the end of the sentence.
examples: The car was cheap, and it came with new tires to boot.
He's a fine cook, and a patient teacher to boot.
The house needs a roof, a furnace, and rewiring to boot.
She won the election, and carried two neighboring counties to boot.
The place was noisy, cramped, and overpriced to boot.
They refunded the tickets, and threw in a voucher for next season to boot.
entries.русский: в придачу, вдобавок — разг., слегка старомодно и с иронией; только в конце фразы
entries.register: informal to neutral; old-fashioned in flavor and faintly wry, at home in speech, reviews, and feature writing, and out of place in business or technical prose
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (a clause-final additive tag; the boot in it is the obsolete noun bōt "advantage, something extra", unrelated to footwear and surviving elsewhere only in bootless "useless")
entries.clause type: coordinate tag — closes a clause by throwing in one last item
entries.pattern: [clause], and [final item] to boot. · [X], [Y], and [Z] to boot. · [adjective], and [second adjective] to boot. · [noun phrase] to boot.
entries.punctuation: Comma before the added item, no comma between that item and to boot, and nothing after it — the tag ends the sentence (He was late, and rude to boot). It never joins two clauses by itself: put and in front of the second element, or start a new sentence.
entries.variants: besides · as well · in the bargain (American) · into the bargain (chiefly British) · for good measure · and then some (of quantities rather than items)
entries.see also: as well, and then some, not to mention, on top of that, over and above, besides

entries.meaning: The written, faintly rhetorical cousin of not to mention: it adds one more item under cover of declining to raise it. Like not to mention it needs no negative ahead of it and does not rank the two items on a scale, which is exactly what separates it from let alone, much less, and still less.
examples: The renovation swallowed our savings, to say nothing of two summers.
He lost the account, to say nothing of the goodwill that came with it.
The plan would take a decade, to say nothing of the money.
She managed the move alone, to say nothing of the paperwork it involved.
The heat was punishing, to say nothing of the mosquitoes.
The bridge closure cost the county millions — to say nothing of the two years drivers spent sitting in traffic.
entries.русский: не говоря уже о — книжн. вариант not to mention
entries.register: formal to neutral; chiefly written
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (distinct from the literal infinitive to say nothing of: She chose to say nothing of the argument)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase (an add-on)
entries.pattern: [independent clause], to say nothing of [noun phrase]. · [X], to say nothing of [Y]. · [independent clause] — to say nothing of [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: Comma before to say nothing of, no comma after it. A dash or a pair of parentheses reads better when the add-on runs long or lands as an aside.
entries.variants: not to mention (neutral) · never mind (informal) · let alone (only after a negative) · to say nothing about (rare)
entries.see also: not to mention, never mind, let alone, much less, as well as

entries.meaning: Sets two things against each other as opposed alternatives — a real contest (Yankees versus Red Sox) or a choice being argued about (speed versus accuracy). Unlike or, it does not offer a choice so much as frame a comparison, and it cannot join two finite clauses.
examples: Tonight it's the Yankees versus the Red Sox.
The whole debate comes down to speed versus accuracy.
We compared the cost of repairing the roof versus replacing it.
Ohio State vs. Michigan is the only game he cares about.
Every first-year law student reads Brown v. Board of Education.
It's a question of quantity versus quality.
entries.русский: против, в сравнении с — сталкивает две стороны; юр. и спорт.
entries.register: neutral; fixed and formal in legal and sports citation
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (a preposition by strict analysis)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase — joins noun phrases and, informally, -ing clauses; never finite clauses
entries.pattern: [X] versus [Y]. · [X] vs. [Y]. · [Party] v. [Party]. (case names)
entries.punctuation: No commas around it. Abbreviate as vs. in general American prose and v. in the names of legal cases (Roe v. Wade); American style keeps the period on both, where British style often drops it.
entries.variants: vs. · v. (legal) · versus spelled out; the spelling verses is a different word entirely
entries.see also: or, rather than, as opposed to, minus, times, whereas

entries.meaning: Climbs from the word just used to a stronger one and keeps both: a generous offer, yea, an extravagant one asserts generosity and then outbids it with extravagance. Its twin nay withdraws the first word instead of keeping it (a good, nay, a great man). Both belong to scripture, older oratory, and writing that means to sound like them.
examples: It was a generous offer, yea, an extravagant one.
He served the town for thirty years, yea, for the better part of his life.
The work is difficult, yea, all but impossible for one person.
She was a friend to him, yea, the only friend he had.
They gave what they could spare, yea, more than they could spare.
The road was long, yea, longer than any of us had reckoned.
entries.русский: более того, да что там — устар., книжн.: усиливает сказанное, не отменяя его
entries.register: archaic, literary; scripture, older oratory, and deliberate pastiche
entries.type: quasi-coordinator (archaic, intensifying; distinct from the yea of voice votes — the yeas and nays — and from informal yeah /ˈjɛə/)
entries.clause type: coordinate phrase or clause — introduces a stronger restatement of what was just said
entries.pattern: [X], yea, [stronger X]. · [clause], yea, [stronger clause]. · [adjective], yea, [stronger adjective]. · compare corrective [X], nay, [replacement X].
entries.punctuation: Fence it with a comma on each side: it interrupts rather than linking two halves that could stand alone. Sentence-initial Yea in older texts takes its own comma after it.
entries.variants: nay (the corrective twin — it replaces the first word instead of raising it) · indeed · even · and more than that
entries.see also: nor yet, as also, if not, and, indeed
